# The design limits the questions: identification {#sec-identification}

Suppose we run a proper randomized experiment. We randomly encourage some students — and not others — to study for an upcoming test, and the encouraged group scores higher.^[Randomized *encouragement* rather than randomized studying, because you cannot force a student to study; you can only make studying more likely. Keep this design in mind — it returns near the end of the chapter with a surprising extra use. It is an old workhorse of the methodological literature [@holland1988; @shadish2002].] The effect is real; the design is clean; the first chapter's checklist comes up green. Immediately, everyone in the seminar room asks the same next question: *how does it work?* Does encouragement raise scores because students study more — or through something else, nerves calmed, attention flattered?

That question — does the effect of $X$ on $Y$ run *through* $M$? — is called **mediation**, and it is one of the most-asked questions in the social and health sciences. This chapter uses it as a case study in something bigger. The previous chapter ended with a warning: a model that fits is not thereby true. Here we meet the hard version. For some questions, *no amount of data* can distinguish truth from a rival story — not because the data are noisy, but because the design never put the answer into the data in the first place. Statisticians call this the problem of "identification", and it is the sharpest illustration in this book of the chain from @sec-rq-to-interpretation: the design determines which assumptions are plausible, and thereby which questions have answers at all.

## The mediation model

By the recipe of @sec-theory-to-glm, the how-does-it-work theory becomes two equations (all variables standardized): encouragement $X$, study time $M$, test score $Y$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
M &= a\,X + \zeta_M \\
Y &= c'\,X + b\,M + \zeta_Y ,
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-mediation}

![The mediation model. The effect of $X$ on $Y$ splits into a direct part ($c'$) and an indirect part through $M$ ($a \times b$).](diagrams/mediation.png){#fig-mediation width="85%" fig-align="center"}

and the tracing rules hand us the payoff immediately. Two traces connect $X$ and $Y$: the direct path, and the path through $M$. So

$$
\underbrace{\rho_{XY}}_{\text{total effect}} = \underbrace{c'}_{\text{direct}} + \underbrace{a\,b}_{\text{indirect}} .
$$

Estimate the equations, multiply $\hat a \hat b$, and you have "the share of the effect that runs through studying." This estimation recipe has circulated in psychology for decades under the name of @baron1986; the recipe is not our subject — what the numbers *mean* is.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 3.1"}
In a study of education ($X$), health knowledge ($M$), and longevity ($Y$): $\hat a = 0.5$, $\hat b = 0.4$, $\hat c' = 0.1$. Compute the indirect, direct, and total effects and the "proportion mediated". Then say in one sentence what the indirect effect claims about the world, if the model is true.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 3.1"}
Indirect $= .5 \times .4 = .20$; direct $= .10$; total $= .30$; proportion mediated $= 2/3$. The claim: two-thirds of education's benefit for longevity would come about *because* education raises health knowledge, which raises longevity — so an intervention on health knowledge alone could capture most of the benefit. Feel the size of that claim; the rest of the chapter asks what entitles anyone to it.
:::

## The assumptions behind the arrows

Equations [-@eq-mediation] are claims, and by now you know where credibility must come from. Reading $\hat a$, $\hat b$, $\hat c'$ causally requires, besides linearity: **no $X$–$M$ confounding**; **no $M$–$Y$ confounding** (the disturbances $\zeta_M$ and $\zeta_Y$ uncorrelated); and **correct causal order** — the arrows point the way drawn.

Here is mediation's trap. Randomizing $X$ — the strongest design feature we own — buys the first assumption completely: a coin flip has no common causes with anything. It buys *nothing* for the other two. Nobody randomized study time. Within each arm of our experiment, the students who studied a lot are simply *different people* from those who studied little — perhaps more conscientious, better rested, less distracted — and any of that may drive test scores on its own. Look at the trap in the equations: $\zeta_M$ and $\zeta_Y$ both collect "everything else" about a student, and the model assumes those two everything-elses are unrelated. The $b$ path is an observational study smuggled inside a randomized experiment.

Rather than warn you about the consequences, let me have you watch them happen twice — the promised failures one and two.

## Failure one: the arrows can be backwards

We simulate a world where our model is exactly true — encouragement raises study time ($a = 0.5$), studying raises scores ($b = 0.4$), no direct effect — and fit two models: the true one, and a model with every arrow reversed (scores drive studying, studying drives... encouragement).

```{r}
#| label: reversed-arrows
library(lavaan)
set.seed(4)
n <- 1000
X <- as.numeric(scale(rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)))          # randomized encouragement
M <- 0.5 * X + rnorm(n, sd = sqrt(1 - 0.25))       # study time
Y <- 0.4 * M + rnorm(n, sd = sqrt(1 - 0.16))       # test score
d <- data.frame(X, M, Y)

fit_true     <- sem("M ~ X \n Y ~ M", data = d)
fit_reversed <- sem("M ~ Y \n X ~ M", data = d)

c(true = fitMeasures(fit_true, "chisq"),
  reversed = fitMeasures(fit_reversed, "chisq"))
```

The simulation builds the world; the two `sem()` calls fit the rival stories; the last line prints their chi-square fit statistics. They are **identical**. Not close — identical to every decimal, in this dataset and in every dataset either model will ever meet.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 3.2"}
Before reading on, explain the result using what @sec-theory-to-glm taught about what a path model implies for correlations. Hint: what does each model imply about $\rho_{XY}$?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 3.2"}
Each chain model has three parameters facing three observed correlations and imposes exactly one constraint. Trace it: the chain $X \rightarrow M \rightarrow Y$ implies $\rho_{XY} = \rho_{XM}\,\rho_{MY}$ — the only trace from $X$ to $Y$ runs through $M$. The reversed chain $Y \rightarrow M \rightarrow X$ implies... $\rho_{XY} = \rho_{MY}\,\rho_{XM}$. The same constraint. Both models say "the outer correlation is the product of the inner two" and are silent about direction. Since they restrict the observable correlations identically, no data can prefer one — their entire disagreement lives in claims the data cannot see.
:::

This situation has a name. Two models (or two parameter values) are **not identified** when they imply the same distribution of observable data: the data then have no opinion, however many of them you collect. The term sounds technical and mildly bureaucratic; what it names is the mathematical form of a limit on knowledge.^[@saris1984 note that such a model is "unidentified, or perhaps more appropriately, unidentifiable" — the answer is not hiding in the data; it is not in there. They also give the useful counting diagnostic: a model with more parameters than observed variances-plus-covariances cannot possibly be identified. But counting is only necessary, not sufficient, as the reversed-arrows pair shows: both count fine, and the *direction* is still not identified.] And remember the closing worry of @sec-theory-to-glm — with seven variables, five-thousand-odd saturated models all fit perfectly [@saris1984]. Those models disagree with each other about the causal story; the data shrug.

Can anything break the tie? Yes — the design, which is the point of this chapter. Because $X$ was randomized, an arrow *into* $X$ is absurd: study time cannot cause a coin flip. The reversed model dies — killed by the design, not by the fit statistic. But watch how far that victory extends: the coin flip orients only $X$'s own edges. For the $M$–$Y$ pair we measured two variables and randomized neither, so "studying raises scores" and "good students study more" (or a common cause of both) remain observationally identical. The design limits the questions.

## Failure two: the hidden confounder

Now the second assumption. New world: encouragement still raises study time ($a = 0.5$), but studying does *nothing whatsoever* for scores ($b = 0$). Instead an unmeasured trait — call it conscientiousness, $U$ — drives both study time and scores.

```{r}
#| label: hidden-confounder
set.seed(5)
U  <- rnorm(n)                                        # never measured
M2 <- 0.5 * X + 0.6 * U + rnorm(n, sd = sqrt(1 - 0.25 - 0.36))
Y2 <- 0.0 * M2 + 0.6 * U + rnorm(n, sd = sqrt(1 - 0.36))
d2 <- data.frame(X, M = M2, Y = Y2)

round(coef(sem("M ~ X \n Y ~ M + X", data = d2)), 2)
```

The mediation analysis reports a healthy, "highly significant" $\hat b \approx 0.48$, and a referee would read that most of the encouragement effect is "mediated by study time." Every number is precisely estimated. Every causal number is wrong. In this world, an intervention on studying achieves nothing — studying does not cause scores; conscientiousness just makes the two travel together inside each experimental arm. Notice also $\hat c' \approx -0.25$: a spurious *negative* "direct effect", conjured by the same confounder to balance the books.^[The books must balance because the total effect $\rho_{XY}$ is honestly estimated — $X$ is randomized — so when the indirect share is inflated, the direct share is pushed down to compensate. Analysts then earnestly interpret the negative direct path ("encouragement backfires unless you study!"). It is an accounting artifact.] More data would tighten the intervals around the wrong values. This is the wine-drinkers study of @sec-rq-to-interpretation reborn inside a randomized experiment.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 3.3"}
Explain with a trace through $X \rightarrow M \leftarrow U \rightarrow Y$ why regressing $Y$ on $M$ and $X$ produces a nonzero coefficient on $M$ although $M$ does not cause $Y$ — and why randomizing $X$ did not protect us.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 3.3"}
$M$ and $Y$ share the common cause $U$: high-$U$ students study more *and* score higher, so $M$ and $Y$ are correlated at every level of $X$. Regression can only redescribe that correlation, and books it under the $M$ coefficient. In model terms, $U$ sits in both $\zeta_M$ and $\zeta_Y$, so the disturbances are correlated — the no-$M$–$Y$-confounding assumption fails. Randomization guarantees $U$ is unrelated to $X$ — which is why $\hat a$ is fine and the *total* effect of $X$ is fine — but it constrains nothing about $U$'s relation to $M$ or $Y$. The coin flip protects only the variable it assigned.
:::

## Trading one assumption for another: instrumental variables

So far, demolition. Now the constructive turn — and it is a beautiful one.

Stay in the confounded world, but be honest in the model: allow the disturbances to covary. Draw a curved arc between $\zeta_M$ and $\zeta_Y$ and call its value $\psi_{MY}$ — the confounding, given a parameter of its own. Count, as @saris1984 taught: observables $\rho_{XM}, \rho_{XY}, \rho_{MY}$ — three; unknowns $a, b, c', \psi_{MY}$ — four. One short. Not identified, and this time the counting rule alone convicts.

But suppose the theory can honestly assert **no direct effect**: encouragement moves scores *only* by moving study time, $c' = 0$. Trace what remains: $\rho_{XM} = a$, and $\rho_{XY} = a b$ — the only surviving trace to $Y$ runs through $M$ (the curved arc is not a causal path from $X$). Divide:

$$
b = \frac{\rho_{XY}}{\rho_{XM}} .
$$

Three observables, three unknowns ($a$, $b$, $\psi_{MY}$), and $b$ is identified *without assuming away the confounding* — $\psi_{MY}$ is now estimated from the data rather than assumed to be zero. Read the trade in plain terms: **we swapped "no $M$–$Y$ confounding" for "no direct effect".** Neither is testable here; the swap is struck entirely on theoretical credit. When it is credible, $X$ gets a new job title: an **instrumental variable** — we are not interested in encouragement itself; we use its randomness as a lever to wiggle study time and watch what happens to scores [@angrist1996].

Does it work? In the very dataset that fooled the mediation analysis:

```{r}
#| label: iv-estimate
model_iv <- "
  M ~ a * X
  Y ~ b * M
  M ~~ Y        # disturbances may covary: confounding allowed
"
round(coef(sem(model_iv, data = d2))[c("a", "b")], 2)
round(cov(d2$X, d2$Y) / cov(d2$X, d2$M), 2)   # the same, by hand
```

The model string forbids the direct path, frees the disturbance covariance (`M ~~ Y`), and the estimate lands essentially on the truth: $\hat b \approx -0.06 \approx 0$ — studying does nothing, correctly reported, from confounded data. The second line shows the whole apparatus reduces to one division.

Now the fine print, printed large. First, that division has $\rho_{XM}$ in the denominator: **the instrument must move the mediator, and not feebly.** With a weak instrument the estimator divides noise by almost-zero:

```{r}
#| label: weak-instrument
#| fig-cap: "IV estimates across 500 simulated studies (n = 1000, true b = 0). Left: a strong instrument. Right: a weak one — same estimator, now wild (estimates clipped at ±10)."
one_iv <- function(a) {
  U <- rnorm(1000); X <- rnorm(1000)
  M <- a * X + 0.6 * U + rnorm(1000)
  Y <- 0.6 * U + rnorm(1000)
  cov(X, Y) / cov(X, M)
}
set.seed(6)
strong <- replicate(500, one_iv(0.5))
weak   <- replicate(500, one_iv(0.05))
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hist(strong, main = "Strong (a = 0.5)", xlab = "IV estimate of b",
     breaks = 30); abline(v = 0, lwd = 2)
hist(pmax(pmin(weak, 10), -10), main = "Weak (a = 0.05)",
     xlab = "IV estimate of b", breaks = 30); abline(v = 0, lwd = 2)
```

Weak instruments do not merely widen intervals; they make the estimator erratic, and, when the instrument is even slightly invalid, badly biased [@bound1995]. Second, the exclusion restriction $c' = 0$ is untestable in these data and does real work. If encouragement also calms nerves — a second active ingredient — the "instrument" smuggles a direct effect into the numerator, and $\hat b$ is quietly corrupted.

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 3.4"}
State the three requirements for $X$ to instrument the effect of $M$ on $Y$; for each, name what could support it in the encouragement example. Which one does randomization buy?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 3.4"}
(1) *Relevance*: $X$ moves $M$, non-feebly — checkable from $\hat\rho_{XM}$, and improvable by choosing stronger encouragement. (2) *Exogeneity*: $X$ shares no common causes with $Y$ — bought by randomization, and by randomization alone among our tools. (3) *Exclusion*: $X$ touches $Y$ only through $M$ — bought by nothing in the design; it is a theoretical claim about the mechanism of encouragement (and doubtful, if encouragement also reassures). An instrument is exactly as credible as the argument for its exclusion restriction.
:::

## Instruments in the wild

Where do good instruments come from? Sometimes we *build* them: the encouragement design is precisely a machine for manufacturing instruments — randomize the nudge, then use it as a lever on the behavior you could not randomize [@holland1988]. The same logic runs any trial with imperfect compliance: assignment is randomized, treatment received is not; assignment instruments treatment received.

Sometimes nature or bureaucracy randomizes for us. The Vietnam draft lottery randomly encouraged military service. Quarter of birth, through school-entry rules, nudged some children into slightly more schooling [@angrist1991]. And in **Mendelian randomization**, the genetic lottery at conception serves as the randomizer: variants that raise alcohol consumption, say, are dealt out plausibly independently of lifestyle confounders, and instrument the exposure's effect on disease [@daveysmith2003].

Every example inherits the same fine print, usually in a local dialect. The draft lottery instruments service only if lottery numbers touched later outcomes *solely* through service — yet draft avoidance kept some men in university, an education path around the treatment: an exclusion violation flagged by @shadish2002. Quarter of birth is the canonical *weak* instrument, the case study that launched the weak-instrument literature [@bound1995]. In Mendelian randomization the exclusion worry is "pleiotropy" — one gene, many pathways — and modern MR practice is largely a battery of partial defenses against it [@davies2018]; genes also come dealt unevenly across ancestries that differ in other ways, so the meiotic lottery is fair only within families or well-stratified samples. And there is a subtler limit, raised politely by @angrist1996 and pointedly by @deaton2010: an instrument moves only the units it moves — "compliers" — so even a valid instrument answers a narrower question than the one usually asked, the effect *among those the nudge budged*, not in the population. Valid answers to slightly different questions: the design relocated the limit; it did not remove it.

Mediation analysis, meanwhile, carries its own bill of indictment. In psychology, where the $b$ path is routinely estimated from unrandomized mediators measured minutes before the outcome, methodologists have argued that a large share of published mediation claims rest on assumptions nobody stated, let alone defended [@bullock2010; @rohrer2022]. The remedy is not to abandon the how-does-it-work question — mechanism *is* often the scientific question — but to treat the mediation model as this book treats every model: as a set of assumptions waiting for a design. Randomize the mediator when you can; instrument it when you credibly can; measure the confounders you can name; and state the causal claim with the modesty its warrant has earned.

## Reading the chapter backwards

Identification is a property of the question–design pair — not of the estimator, the sample size, or the software. The mediation story taught the general lessons in miniature:

- Two opposite models fit identically: the data cannot orient an edge the design did not orient.
- A hidden confounder made every estimate precise and wrong: assumptions the design does not buy fail *silently*.
- One untestable assumption bought back identification: assumptions are currency, and the design sets the exchange rate.
- The instrument's own fine print — relevance, exclusion, compliers — moved the limits rather than abolishing them.

When you meet an analysis, any analysis, the identification question is the fifth checklist question of @sec-rq-to-interpretation asked with maximal severity: *which feature of the design put the answer to this question into the data at all?* If none did, no estimator will get it out.

## Test yourself {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 3.A"}
A published RCT randomized a workplace exercise program ($X$), measured sleep quality ($M$) at 3 months and burnout ($Y$) at 6 months. Standardized estimates: $\hat a = 0.4$, $\hat b = 0.5$, $\hat c' = 0.1$ (n.s.). The authors conclude: "the program's effect on burnout is fully mediated by sleep; workplaces could target sleep directly."

(a) Compute the implied indirect and total effects.
(b) List the assumptions the "fully mediated" reading needs, and say which this design supports.
(c) Construct a concrete alternative world producing these same estimates in which targeting sleep does nothing for burnout.
(d) The authors argue that measuring $M$ before $Y$ establishes causal order. Evaluate.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 3.A"}
(a) Indirect $= .20$; total $= .30$. (b) No $X$–$M$ or $X$–$Y$ confounding: bought by randomization. No $M$–$Y$ confounding: not bought — sleep was never randomized. Correct $M \rightarrow Y$ order: not established (see d). Linearity/additivity: assumed by convention. (c) Let the program build an unmeasured "recovery capacity" $U$ that improves both sleep and burnout, with no sleep $\rightarrow$ burnout arrow: within arms $U$ correlates $M$ with $Y$ (yielding $\hat b \approx .5$), the program moves sleep through $U$ ($\hat a \approx .4$), the direct path absorbs little. A sleep-only intervention then changes burnout not at all. (d) Measurement order rules out *this* $Y$ measurement causing *this* $M$ measurement — nothing more. Burnout is chronic: baseline burnout (absent from the model) may drive both 3-month sleep and 6-month burnout. Temporal order of measurements is not causal order of variables.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 3.B"}
An epidemiologist uses a genetic variant that slows alcohol metabolism ($G$) as an instrument for the effect of alcohol consumption ($M$) on esophageal cancer ($Y$).

(a) Draw the assumed model; write the IV estimate of $b$ as a ratio of correlations.
(b) State the three instrument requirements in genetic terms.
(c) The variant also causes facial flushing, which reduces drinking but also correlates with other health behaviors through ancestry. Which requirements are threatened, and what are the MR-dialect terms?
(d) The variant is common in one subpopulation, rare in another, and the subpopulations differ in diet. Explain the bias and name one remedy.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 3.B"}
(a) $G \rightarrow M \rightarrow Y$, disturbance arc $\zeta_M \leftrightarrow \zeta_Y$ free, no $G \rightarrow Y$ arrow; $\hat b = \rho_{GY}/\rho_{GM}$. (b) Relevance: the variant shifts consumption. Exogeneity: the variant is dealt independently of confounders of drinking and cancer — the meiotic-lottery argument. Exclusion: the variant reaches cancer only through consumption. (c) A second pathway from the variant to the outcome violates exclusion: "(horizontal) pleiotropy" [@davies2018]. The ancestry route violates exogeneity: the lottery was not fair across strata. (d) That is "population stratification": subpopulation membership causes both variant frequency and, via diet, cancer risk — a confounder of the instrument itself. Remedies: genetically homogeneous samples, adjustment for genetic principal components, or within-family designs, where the meiotic lottery argument holds exactly.
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false" title="Exercise 3.C"}
Return to the reversed-arrows demonstration. A colleague proposes: "Chains are ambiguous — fine. I will fit all three models ($X \rightarrow M \rightarrow Y$; $Y \rightarrow M \rightarrow X$; and the common-cause model $X \leftarrow M \rightarrow Y$) and report whichever fits best."

(a) Derive the constraint on correlations implied by the common-cause model; compare it to the chains'.
(b) What will the colleague find, and why does the strategy fail?
(c) Now let $X$ be randomized. Which models die, on what grounds, and what stays unresolved?
(d) State the general lesson in one sentence using this chapter's vocabulary.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Answer 3.C"}
(a) In $X \leftarrow M \rightarrow Y$ the single trace between $X$ and $Y$ goes backward then forward through $M$: $\rho_{XY} = \rho_{XM}\rho_{MY}$ — the same constraint as both chains. (b) All three fit identically in every possible dataset; "best fit" selects noise. The models are observationally equivalent: they differ only in claims that leave no fingerprint on the data's distribution. (c) Randomization kills every arrow into $X$ — the reversed chain and the common-cause model both die, by design, not by fit. Whether the surviving $M$–$Y$ edge reflects $M \rightarrow Y$, confounding, or reverse causation remains exactly as open as before. (d) Model comparison is no substitute for identification: when the design leaves rivals observationally equivalent, the data have no opinion, at any sample size.
:::
